battle.title: Process or Thread? The Great Divide
battle.description: Address spaces, shared memory and context switches: who owns what?

questions.text: Two threads belong to the same process. Which of these do they share?
options: The heap and open files of the process
questions.answer: The heap and open files of the process
questions.explanation: Threads share the process address space (code, globals, heap) and resources like open files. Each thread still has its own stack, registers and program counter, so it can run independently.

questions.text: Which statement about context switching is generally true?
options: Switching threads and switching processes always cost the same
Switching threads is cheaper than switching between processes
Switching processes is cheaper because they are isolated
Threads never need a context switch
questions.answer: Switching threads is cheaper than switching between processes
questions.explanation: A switch between threads of one process keeps the same address space, so no page-table change and fewer TLB and cache penalties. A process switch must swap address spaces, which is why it costs more.

questions.text: A web browser must ensure that a crash in one tab cannot corrupt memory in other tabs. Which design fits best?
options: Run each tab in its own process
Run each tab as a thread in one process
Run all tabs in one thread and take turns
Share one heap and guard it with comments
questions.answer: Run each tab in its own process
questions.explanation: Processes have separate address spaces, so a faulty tab cannot overwrite another tab's memory. Threads share the heap, so a stray write or crash in one thread can take down the others.
The array lives on the heap, which both threads share, so the worker's change is visible to main. join() guarantees the worker finished before the print: 2 * 5 = 10.

questions.text: One thread of a multi-threaded native program dereferences an invalid pointer and triggers a segmentation fault. What typically happens?
options: Only that thread ends and the others carry on
The OS pauses the thread until it is fixed
The whole process is terminated, along with all its threads
Only the main thread is killed
questions.answer: The whole process is terminated, along with all its threads
questions.explanation: A fault is delivered to the process, and the default action kills it entirely. Threads share one address space and have no isolation from each other, which is exactly the trade-off against separate processes.
